Solomzi Nqweni : Not a solo journey

By: Sinethemba Nogude | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A promising cricket career curtailed by a rare autoimmune disorder.We speak to all-rounder Solomzi Nqweni's as he takes us through his remarkable journey to recovery.

Unique Selling Point:
A budding cricketing career with the promise of donning the green and gold...First-class cricketer hoped his dream of representing South Africa on a global stage would be realized one day...A stint at Aberdeenshire Cricket club in Scotland would be a perfect steppingstone...but fate had other ideas : It was a typically glooming day in Scotland 'Solo' been representing Aberdeenshire Cricket Club at its ground in Mannofield in Aberdeen, playing against Arbroath on the 14 of July 2019 .

After a bowling day to forget m, he returned to his flat unaware that his life was about to change forever...He contracted a very rare autoimmune disorder called Guillain -Barre Syndrome...( you are more likely to space than get Guillain Barre Syndrome) where your own immune system attacks your nerves rendering you completely paralysed- Many suffered have described this as "being a prisoner of your own body".

Solo would spend 6 months in ICU...in and out of induced comas... during that period he suffered liver and kidney failure because of his compromised immunity...but despite the odds being heavily stacked against him the resilient bowler was putting on a brave fight in what was the greatest 'test' of his life.

Solo had to undergone extensive treatment to revive his speech and mobility, and after giving himself just a year to walk again... He would realize this goal and took his first tentative steps after a year.


This is a story of resilience under the overwhelming circumstances and despite his chances of playing professional cricket again being slim...Solo still holds on to a dream of making a run-up to the stumps one day.

Treatment :
The story will rely a lot on footage taken by Solo's family- this will give viewers an insight into his journey. I want to tell the story as a 'Heroes'journey'...(as cliche as that may be) Our protagonist ( Solomzi) is dealt a bad hand, his situation seems insurmountable ( Solo contracts a rare-autoimmune disorder)... and as fate would have it he has to embark on an arduous journey with many obstacles in the way ( In Solo's case he had to fight various protagonists- Guillian Barre Syndrome, Liver failure and Kidney failure) and on this journey he discovers the strength within... and with the help of various aides ( in Solo's case - NHS doctors , His mother Zandile,his friend Peter Gerard and his physio Sharon) he is able to to reach his goal-something many of us take for granted... Just being able to walk.

Script:


Solo Nqweni : Not a solo Journey
Opening scene: Solo walking into the stadium – cuts to visuals from the back – cuts to walking stick- - cuts to Solo watching cricket contemplating - -- cuts to cricketing visuals – cuts back to solo—But that dream was taken away from me …pause – fast pace cut with cellphone footage, cricket footage—fades into black— Stirring music laid.
--- Breathing room---
V/O Many young cricketers dream of wearing the Proteas green and gold and playing on the world stage, for Solomzi Nqweni his dream was to follow in the footsteps of cricketing icons like Jacque Kallis and Makhaya Ntini
Upsound : Upsound : 01 :01 I studied the greats //I used to watch videos before training // 01 hr :08 I wanted to play for South Africa at the highest level, go to a World Cup win a World Cup.
Claire’s question: When did you realize you were good?
Upsound Solomzi : 06:09 When I was around 15/16// I started getting selected for national teams and camps on a national level where you are training with the top 30 players in your age group in the country and you are holding your own
V/O Nqweni would excel with the ball playing for the Eastern Province cricket team and representing South Africa at the 2012 under 19 World cup in Australia. before Going on to play first class cricket for Aberdeenshire Cricket Club in Scotland.
Breather- cricketing visuals
V/O But on the 15 July 2019 his life would change forever.
Upsound : 13:32 That day was actually the day of the cricket world cup between New Zealand and England // 12:45 I played a match on the Saturday, probably one of my best games of the season, I had a long day of bowling and batting…I felt normally fatigued , on the Sunday morning …I noticed that my grip of the coffee mug wasn’t the same…felt weaker than usual //13 :33 Fast forward to a few hours // As I am trying to get off the couch I realized I cant 17:29 I literally said I will wake up tomorrow and everything will be fine
V/O But he wasnt fine.
Upsound Solo : 17:41 Around 2 Am I needed to go to the bathroom, at this stage I had deteriorated even further and I am even weaker //17:51 Fighting to get off the couch, I fell off and rolled on the ground, that when I started screaming //18:23 I had to do this combat thing to try and get to my phone , as I tried to reach my phone //18 :44 My fingers started going , I couldn’t type properly … I had to type like this…. //18:30 At this moment I thought you must be joking.
V/O Nqweni managed to reach his phone and called his roommate Callum Mackaness before losing consciousness.
Upsound Solo: 20 :55 that was the last thing I sort of remembered before then waking up in ICU. Only my eyes moving, whole body shut down tubes everywhere, machines everywhere
V/O: Nqweni was diagnosed with a rare auto-immune disorder- Guillain Barre Syndrome
Link Guillan Barre syndrome or GBS is a rare condition in which your body’s immune system attacks your nerves. Weakness and tingling in your hands and feet are usually the first tell tale symptoms, but that can quickly spread eventually paralyzing your body.
Vo Though the exact cause of GBS is unknown, most people eventually make a full recovery ,but Nqweni’s case was severe.
---Visuals in Hospital- breather --- visuals in hospital
V/O For six months, he would fight for his life at the Aberdeen Royal Hospital in Scotland, this was the greatest test of his life.
Upsound Solo : 29 :19 As a result of the bad state secondary illnesses started coming out. I got tuberculosis my liver and kidney failed as well. So I had to go on dialysis. And then that's the point where they pretty much put me on in an induced coma.
Upsound Aunt Nomkitha : 42 :04 I would actually never forget walking into that room with my mom and dad. Like my dad was broken. Sure.
V/O For the Nqweni family this was a trying time, especially for his grandparents who he had a close relationship with.
Upsound Aunt Nomkitha :29 :20 He was hooked up to every possible machine that you can think of// 29:26 and it was not looking good.
Claire : 42: 47 As a mother, the great parents will they see that? It's an unnatural way for you to see your grandchild or your child.
Upsound Zandile Mother : I cried. Then I walked out of the ICU. and I prayed to God, because I was like, I never expected this reality// Sometimes there'll be days where I'm like, can I exchange because I can see this pain.So maybe I can trade places with him. So that, you know, he doesn't have to go, you know, through this.
V/O Despite doctor’s fears , he pulled through and after 6 months was given the green light to return home and continue his recovery. His aunt Zintathu Nqweni oversaw his repatriation.

Upsound Zintathu Aunt : 49 :13 So throughout the journey,you celebrate all your wins,part of that excitement is finally coming home. //But it was hard because and you think about some of the things because you know, you can't sit around for more than an hour to two and a half hours, how do you prepare you mentally for the physical pain that he is having?
—-Breather— Visuals of Nqweni being wheeeled out of hospital.

Upsound Solo : 38:41 So I traveled with a doctor and a nurse and they literally had to transfer me on to all these different like … into that chain to this ambulance it was very uncomfortable// 40:06 I did realize that me leaving the hospital was one step closer to me recovering.

Link A professional athlete understands the rigorous training regimen required to perform at their best.It would be be in Solo’s journey to recovery where he would have to train harder than ever before.

V/ O Nqweni had to re-learn simple tasks like sitting up,walking and even swallowing.

Upsound Solo: 35 :04 I struggled for a long time, I was depressed for a long time. But then at some point along the way, I just realized that that mindset was, like holding me back.

V/O It was his steely determination and a dedicated rehabilitation team which included Hayley Heslop and Sharon Maritz that helped him progress.

Visuals of Solo recovery excercises

Upsound Hayley Biokineticist : a patient first comes in sees me with GBS, they have muscle wasting and atrophy sort of all over from head to toe // We also did a lot of functional steps to start off with so sitting and standing, . And then we moved on to more sort of his walking and his balance.

Upsound Hayley 14 :12 : Yeah, so he was a good patient, he did work hard, which I think definitely came from his sort of sporting background, always training, always working on his body, he understood that, you know, you need to look after yourself// 14:23 we did have to push a few times. But it's all sort of, you know, he managed to carry on pushing and carry on working through

Claire question : Sharon what were the milestoned for you

Upsound Sharon Physio 05:27 The first time he walked on a treadmill, that was quite amazing. He wasn't a harness, but he was upright, and he was moving his legs on his own.So I just had my hand at his back. know, those those big things for physio, it's amazing to see that kind of thing.
V/O Knocked down in the prime of his life, Solomzi has had to pick up the pieces and chart a new course in the corporate world.
Upsound Solo : 01:09 :16 I had to understand that, as far as I got was as far as I was ever going to be, you know, and I mean, it's hard. It's not easy to accept that because especially when you feel like you have more to offer or had more to offer, I feel like it's unfinished. But I think I've just diverted that energy into into what I'm doing now. Wanting to be the best property developer. quarterly
—Breather—
V/O Documenting his recovery on social media thousands of people around the world keenly following his progress
Claire : Why did you choose to share your journey so publicly, very vulnerable moments ?
Upsound Solo 47 :22 : The more I shared, the more positive positive energy came out of it. And the more I was like, Okay, I got so many people supporting me and rooting for me to get better, actually can't let them down, I actually have an obligation to,
Screen grabs of Solo’s twitter page.
Upsound 47 :33 On the days when I don't feel like going to therapy and feel like doing occupational therapy or wherever I actually I actually have an obligation of because it's not just me, it's not just my family, there's other people that are interested in, what my recovery.
VO One of those people was businessman ,Peter Gerard, who was also recovering from GBS, the two instantly formed a friendship.
Upsound Solo: 01:01:01 I meet this old guy who would come and visit me in hospital, like twice, three times a week had this funny walk was full of jokes, and yet also had the illness that I had. And he was pretty much just giving me energy, really, and really just being a jerky character and educating me on the illness and what he did to to help himself get better. and what fast tracked his progress.
Upsound Peter : In Sollo I saw a bit of myself
Upsound family: 01:06:40 I'm overwhelmed and humbled by the fact that people care about someone we love so much and so deeply, but there's a part of me that's like the human element of it. That's what connects all of us that you're able to watch a story with someone stacked against him, all the odds, and you wrote with them, e did that through family, and it's normal people like that can bring healing to what others to be like, Yo, check guys, and so far, like, we can also find even me, even me, and I think that's what it is. It's a beautiful, triumphant story.
Upsound Family: 01;01:30 we've also grown from Solomzi, his resilience and strength, you know, we feed off that he pushed because he pushes.
Upsound family 56:49 Solomzi courage, because he had, you know, he has the will and determination to want to get better. At times, he didn't believe it himself. But there was just an inner fighting resilience thing in him
08 3 543 9829
natanya
V/O Determined , resolute and unyielding …Solomzi road to recovery has inspired many across the globe and alThough he will never realise his childhood dream of playing for the Proteas he hopes his journey holds lessons for others.
Upsound Solomzi: 01:04 :49 I think maybe towards the end of my life, I will then look back on all the dots that connected along the way. And I'll be able to understand why this happened when it happened. But now was something that I'm just embracing it day by day, understand that there must be some kind of purpose beyond what are currently no in that just simply because of my sharing how far it's gone. And how many people it's impacting in a positive way. And you know what, to me, if something good and positive can come out of this, the end of the day, maybe it wasn't such a bad thing to go through. And maybe my story will be someone else's survival guide on how to navigate difficult times.
— end—

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A promising cricket career curtailed by a rare autoimmune disorder.We speak to all-rounder Solomzi Nqweni's as he takes us through his remarkable journey to recovery.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A budding cricketing career with the promise of donning the green and gold...First-class cricketer hoped his dream of representing South Africa on a global stage would be realized one day...A stint at Aberdeenshire Cricket club in Scotland would be a perfect steppingstone...but fate had other ideas : It was a typically glooming day in Scotland 'Solo' been representing Aberdeenshire Cricket Club at its ground in Mannofield in Aberdeen, playing against Arbroath on the 14 of July 2019 . After a bowling day to forget m, he returned to his flat unaware that his life was about to change forever...He contracted a very rare autoimmune disorder called Guillain -Barre Syndrome...( you are more likely to space than get Guillain Barre Syndrome) where your own immune system attacks your nerves rendering you completely paralysed- Many suffered have described this as "being a prisoner of your own body". Solo would spend 6 months in ICU...in and out of induced comas... during that period he suffered liver and kidney failure because of his compromised immunity...but despite the odds being heavily stacked against him the resilient bowler was putting on a brave fight in what was the greatest 'test' of his life. Solo had to undergone extensive treatment to revive his speech and mobility, and after giving himself just a year to walk again... He would realize this goal and took his first tentative steps after a year. This is a story of resilience under the overwhelming circumstances and despite his chances of playing professional cricket again being slim...Solo still holds on to a dream of making a run-up to the stumps one day. Treatment : The story will rely a lot on footage taken by Solo's family- this will give viewers an insight into his journey. I want to tell the story as a 'Heroes'journey'...(as cliche as that may be) Our protagonist ( Solomzi) is dealt a bad hand, his situation seems insurmountable ( Solo contracts a rare-autoimmune disorder)... and as fate would have it he has to embark on an arduous journey with many obstacles in the way ( In Solo's case he had to fight various protagonists- Guillian Barre Syndrome, Liver failure and Kidney failure) and on this journey he discovers the strength within... and with the help of various aides ( in Solo's case - NHS doctors , His mother Zandile,his friend Peter Gerard and his physio Sharon) he is able to to reach his goal-something many of us take for granted... Just being able to walk.
